citeAs: Paperno, D., Kruszewski, G., Lazaridou, A., Pham, Q. N., Bernardi, R., Pezzelle, S., Baroni, M., Boleda, G., and Fernández, R. (2016). The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. In Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pages 1525–1534, Berlin, Germany.
creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández (CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento; Institute for Logic, Language & Computation, University of Amsterdam)
description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a dataset to evaluate computational models for text understanding via a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages (from the BookCorpus) where human subjects can guess the last word when exposed to the whole passage, but not when only seeing the last sentence. The dataset consists of 10,022 passages (4,869 development and 5,153 test) requiring models to track information across broad discourse context.
name: LAMBADA
publisher: CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento
rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 2 subjects confirmed the target word from the whole passage (steps 1 and 2), plus up to 10 subjects attempted to guess from the sentence alone (step 3).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects evaluated passages via CrowdFlower in three steps: (1) one subject guessed the target word given the whole passage (context + target sentence); if correct, (2) a second subject guessed the target word from the whole passage; if also correct, (3) additional subjects attempted to guess the target word from the target sentence only, with up to 3 guesses per subject, until the word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses were reached. Only passages where no subject could guess the word from the sentence alone were included. Subjects in steps 1 and 2 were paid $0.22 per page (10 passages/page); subjects in step 3 were paid $0.15 per page (20 sentences/page). The same subject was not allowed to judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is heavily biased toward proper nouns (48% of target words) and common nouns (37%), with verbs, adjectives, and adverbs underrepresented compared to the input data distribution. More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context (vs. less than 15% in the unfiltered input). The dataset contains quoted direct speech significantly more often than the unfiltered input (71% vs. 61%). The use of unpublished novels from BookCorpus was intentional to minimize the usefulness of general world knowledge and external resources.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected from the BookCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015), which contains unpublished novels. The corpus (after duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material) contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words. Novels were randomly divided into training and development+testing partitions. Passages were filtered using a combination of four language models to remove easy-to-guess items, then evaluated by human subjects via CrowdFlower crowdsourcing in a three-step pipeline: (1) one subject guesses the target word from the whole passage; (2) a second subject guesses from the whole passage; (3) multiple subjects attempt to guess from the target sentence only (up to 10 unsuccessful guesses). Only passages passing all three steps were included.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw source data is the BookCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015), a collection of unpublished novels. After duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material using a stop word list, the corpus contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to English narrative text from unpublished novels (BookCorpus). The strict hit-or-miss approach (requiring exact word match) excludes passages where synonymous or plausible alternative continuations exist. Cost considerations precluded using more subjects at stage 1, which could in principle improve filtering quality. The dataset is biased toward proper nouns (48% of target words) and common nouns (37%), with verbs, adjectives, and adverbs underrepresented. The test set was initially withheld for a planned competition.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The BookCorpus was preprocessed by removing duplicates and filtering potentially offensive material using a stop word list. Passages were constructed with a context of minimum sentences cumulatively containing at least 50 tokens before the target sentence (context size chosen in a pilot study). Automated filtering removed passages where the target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of four language models (a pre-trained RNN and three models trained on BookCorpus: a 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward model). The vocabulary of models was restricted to the 60K most frequent words in the training set.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to promote research in language models capable of genuine broad-context understanding, which is a fundamental capability for natural language processing systems. By exposing the limitations of state-of-the-art models (none reaching above 1% accuracy), it encourages development of more capable and robust language understanding systems.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating computational models for natural language understanding, specifically their ability to track and use broad discourse context for word prediction. Intended as a challenging benchmark for language models, and as a basis for a public competition to encourage development of models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models were used to filter out easy passages: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2011) and three models trained on the BookCorpus (a standard 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward neural network model). Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of these models was excluded.
